alt: A panel titled What is a Sequence. A sequence is data where the order of the elements matters. I am eating an apple has a meaning, Apple eating am I has the same words but a changed meaning.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled What is the Sequence Learning Problem. The problem is how a neural network can learn from data when the order and previous information matter. A table lists sentence, speech, stock prices, weather readings and music notes with what we want to predict.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled Why can we not simply use a normal neural network. A network that reads words like I did not like this movie independently may miss the relation between not and like, so we need a mechanism that carries information from earlier steps to later steps, which leads to the RNN.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled Why Do We Need RNN. A normal neural network processes I, love and apples separately. A basic feedforward network has no built-in memory of previous inputs, so we need a network that remembers useful information from previous steps.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled RNN, Learning from Previous Information. Current input and previous information go into the RNN and give new information. The words I, love and apples are processed one after another, each with the updated memory.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled RNN Memory becomes Hidden State. The memory carried by an RNN is called the hidden state. Current input and previous hidden state go into the RNN and give a new hidden state.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled RNN Processes One Step at a Time for the sentence I love AI. Step 1 reads I and gives h1, step 2 reads love with h1 and gives h2, step 3 reads AI with h2 and gives h3. The hidden state is updated at every time step.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled Why Recurrent. Recurrent means repeated. Inputs 1 to 4 each go into the RNN, and the previous hidden state is carried forward. Current input plus previous hidden state gives the new hidden state.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Two panels. Left, What Happens Inside an RNN Cell, where the current input x t and previous hidden state h t minus 1 are added and go into the RNN to give the new hidden state h t and the output y t. Right, RNN Complete Basic Flow, repeated for I, love, AI and learning to give h1 to h4.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled Different Ways RNN Can Work, showing many to one (three inputs, one output), one to many (one input, three outputs) and many to many (three inputs, three outputs).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled Many Inputs to One Output. Sentiment analysis of This movie is very good: the RNN reads the whole sequence and gives one final output, Positive. Applications are sentiment analysis, text classification and spam detection.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled One Input to Many Outputs. Image captioning: one image of a boy playing football goes into the RNN, which generates the words A, boy, playing, football one after another.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled Many Inputs to Many Outputs. Language translation of I love AI into J aime l IA, and sequence labelling where each word gets a label.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled Backpropagation Through Time. Time steps t1 to t4 flow forward to the output; after the loss is calculated the error moves backward from t4 to t1. BPTT is backpropagation applied across the different time steps of an RNN.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled How Does BPTT Work for I love AI with four steps: forward pass giving h1, h2, h3 and an output, calculate the loss by comparing the prediction with the actual output, backward pass from the loss through t3, t2 and t1, and update weights using the gradients.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled What Happens with Long Sequences. In a 50 step sequence the gradient has to travel back through all 50 time steps, so it can become very small or very large, leading to the vanishing or exploding gradient.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled Vanishing Gradient. The loss gradient goes 1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001 as it moves backward through time, so earlier time steps receive very little learning signal and the RNN has difficulty learning long-term dependencies.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled Exploding Gradient. The gradient goes 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000 as it moves backward, giving very large weight updates and unstable training. Vanishing means too small, exploding means too large.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled The Long-Term Dependency Problem. I was born in India, many words later I speak Hindi. A basic RNN may struggle to carry the important information India across many time steps.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled Unfolding Computational Graph. The same RNN cell is drawn at four time steps with inputs x1 to x4 and outputs h1 to h4. Unfolding means showing the same RNN cell separately at each time step, and the weights are shared across all time steps.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled Bidirectional RNN. A normal RNN reads x1 to x4 forward and uses information mainly from the past. A bidirectional RNN has a forward and a backward pass and uses information from both directions, as in I went to the bank to deposit money.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled Limitations of Vanilla RNN. It can struggle with long-term dependencies, vanishing gradients, exploding gradients, remembering information from far earlier time steps, and slower training because processing is sequential.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A panel titled Applications of RNN: text and sentiment analysis, next-word prediction, text generation, speech recognition, time-series prediction and music generation. RNN is useful when order and previous information matter.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Two panels from the complete word prediction example. The sequence I love eating with target word pizza, and the forward pass where each word and the previous hidden state give h1, h2 and h3 holding information about I, I love and I love eating.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Two panels from the complete example. A wrong prediction (apple instead of pizza) gives a high loss, and backpropagation through time sends the error backward through h3, h2 and h1 to find the gradients for the weights and biases.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Two panels from the complete example. The weights W, U, b, V and c are updated using the gradients, and on trying again the probability of pizza rises to 90 percent so the prediction matches the target.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A table of two gradient problems. Vanishing gradient: the gradient becomes very small so long-term information is difficult to learn. Exploding gradient: the gradient becomes very large so training becomes unstable. Memory trick: vanishing is too small, exploding is too large.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A flow panel titled Why Does This Happen. During training the RNN uses BPTT; for long sequences gradients can become very small, almost zero; earlier time steps then receive very little learning signal, so the RNN finds it difficult to learn long-term dependencies.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A sheet titled Truncated Backpropagation Through Time. Normal BPTT goes back through all 100 time steps, which is expensive. Truncated BPTT splits the sequence into chunks such as t1 to t4 and t5 to t8 and backpropagates only inside each chunk.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: An unrolled RNN with inputs x of 1, 2, t and t plus 1 at the bottom, outputs y at the top and the activation a passed from step to step, starting from a of 0.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: The RNN equations: a of t equals g1 of W aa times a of t minus 1 plus W ax times x of t plus b a, and y of t equals g2 of W ya times a of t plus b y. The weights W ax, W aa, W ya, b a and b y are shared across time steps.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: The inside of one RNN cell: the previous activation a of t minus 1 is multiplied by W aa, the input x of t by W ax, they are added with the bias b a and passed through g1 to give a of t, which is multiplied by W ya, added to b y and passed through g2 to give y of t.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: An RNN drawn as a loop on the left and unrolled over time on the right. The same weight matrices A (hidden to output), B (input to hidden) and C (hidden to hidden) are used at every time step.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: A recurrent neural network, where each neuron has a loop arrow back to itself, drawn beside a feed-forward neural network, where the neurons have no loops.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: The sequence to sequence model: an encoder made of RNN cells reads x1, x2 and x3 with hidden states, passes the final state as the encoder vector, and a decoder of RNN cells produces y1 and y2.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: Encoder and decoder boxes. The encoder reads the words Welcome to NYC and turns them into numeric vectors which go to the decoder, which starts from a start of sequence word and predicts the next words one by one.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: Encoder and decoder boxes for translation. The decoder starts from the start of sequence word and outputs Bienvenue, then a, then NYC, feeding each predicted word back in as the next input.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: Image captioning: a pretrained CNN turns the input image into a feature vector, a linear layer passes it to a chain of LSTM cells, and each LSTM with a softmax outputs one word of the caption such as Giraffes, standing, until the end token.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: Two hand-drawn plots of derivative size against time step. In exploding gradient the size grows towards plus infinity going back in time. In vanishing gradient it shrinks towards zero going back in time.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut

alt: A syntax tree of the sentence Programming is a lot of fun, with S at the top, N and VP below, and noun phrases NP and word classes DT, N and P at the leaves, as an example of what a recursive neural network works on.
author: Prof. Karishma Raut
